opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what the generated content is actually *for*. When we generate images or videos for people to look at, like art, advertising, or entertainment, the human eye is the final judge. People are very sensitive to texture, lighting and small artifacts, so visual quality is basically the whole product.

When we talk about generation for the physical world, for example a world model that supports a robot or a self-driving system, the consumer isn't a human viewer anymore. It's a policy, a decision-making system. What that system needs is the right structure: where objects are, how they move, what happens when I push this cup or turn this wheel. Physical consistency and causal correctness matter much more than whether every pixel looks photorealistic.

Think about how humans work. When you imagine reaching for a glass of water, you don't render a 4K movie in your head. Your mental picture is blurry and abstract, but it's accurate in the ways that count: distance, weight, the consequence of the action. That kind of "low-fidelity but high-correctness" imagination is enough to act well in the world.

So in my view, chasing visual quality can even be a distraction for embodied intelligence. You spend a lot of compute and model capacity on details that don't change the decision. I'd rather have a model that generates something rough-looking but gets the dynamics and interactions right, and that responds quickly enough for real-time control. Speed, controllability and physical plausibility are the real metrics there, not aesthetics.

That said, I wouldn't say quality doesn't matter at all. If the image is too degraded, you lose information the agent needs. The point is that the bar is set by the task, not by human taste. Once you reframe it that way, a lot of the priorities in generative modeling shift.

r001.rationale: The response says low visual fidelity can suffice when a policy can use correct structure and physical dynamics, but it does not explain that cameras still let us see the generated content.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer in character as the guest, Yujun Shen.

Because in the physical world, the picture is not the product. When we talk about image or video generation for entertainment, the pixels are the end deliverable, so every bit of fidelity matters. A viewer notices blurry hair, a wrong finger, a flickering background. But when a model generates for embodied intelligence, for a robot or an autonomous system, the image is just an intermediate representation. What really matters is whether the model understands the world correctly: where the objects are, how they move, what happens when you push this cup or open that drawer.

Think about how humans work. When you imagine picking up a glass of water, you don't render a photorealistic 4K video in your head. Your mental picture is vague, low-resolution, maybe even black and white. But you grab the glass without spilling it. The imagination is coarse, and the action is precise. That tells us physical interaction depends on the right abstraction, not on high-frequency detail.

There's also a practical side. Robots need to run in real time, often on limited compute. Generating a high-fidelity frame costs a lot, and most of that cost goes toward texture and lighting detail that contributes nothing to the decision. If you spend the compute budget on predicting dynamics, on causality, on consistency across time, you get much more value than spending it on sharper pixels.

So I'd say low image quality is not just acceptable, it's almost the correct design choice. The goal is a world model that is right about physics and cheap to run. Visual beauty is a nice bonus, but for the physical world, it's not what we're optimizing for.

r001.rationale: The response says physical-world generation can use coarse imagery because the image is an intermediate representation and action depends on the right abstraction. It does not explain that low quality is acceptable because cameras still let us see what is generated.

astra-6.text: I think it depends on what we mean by quality. In the physical world, the goal is often to help a system understand what will happen when it takes an action. The generated image doesn’t necessarily need to look beautiful, but it needs to preserve the information that matters: where objects are, how they move, and how they interact. A slightly blurry image can still tell you whether a robot’s gripper will reach an object. A photorealistic image with the wrong geometry may be much less useful. So low visual quality can be acceptable, as long as the generation is accurate enough for the task.

r001.rationale: The response says low visual quality is acceptable when task-relevant information is preserved, but it does not explain that cameras still let us see what is generated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by quality. If we generate an image for people to look at, visual quality matters a lot. But if we generate a scene to train a robot, the goal is to help the robot learn how to act. A beautiful image doesn’t necessarily make that training more useful.

For example, if a robot is learning to pick up a cup, the cup’s geometry, its position, and what happens when the robot touches it may matter more than whether the texture looks photorealistic. You can tolerate relatively simple rendering if those task-relevant properties are correct.

So I wouldn’t say low quality is always acceptable. I would say we need to measure quality differently: does the generated environment help the system learn something that transfers to the real world?

r001.rationale: The response says simplified rendering can be acceptable when task-relevant properties are correct, but it does not explain that cameras let us see what is generated.
